source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Minimum message length
finding: MML was invented by Chris Wallace and first appeared in Wallace and Boulton 1968. First use was mixture models with the best number of classes (Snob). The message is model bits plus data-given-model bits. Parameter precision is traded against fit using Fisher information.
numbers: Dates only: 1968 origin, 1987 Wallace-Freeman approximation. No experiments on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia page, not a primary source. Claims of invariance and consistency (Neyman-Scott) are stated, not shown.
agent_relevance: Gives the two-part cost form we could use to score candidate explanations: cost of the hypothesis plus cost of the evidence given it.

source: Gruenwald (2004) A Tutorial Introduction to the Minimum Description Length Principle
finding: MML predates MDL by about 10 years (Wallace and Boulton 1968, 1975; Wallace and Freeman 1987). MML always uses two-part codes and picks model family and parameters together. MDL codes minimise worst-case regret; MML two-part codes minimise expected code length under a subjective prior. So MML is explicitly Bayesian.
numbers: Comparison figure 2.6 (MDL vs MML vs prequential). No numbers.
limits: Written from the MDL side. Says in practice the two often give similar results.
agent_relevance: MML needs a prior over hypotheses. For an LLM agent the only available prior is the model's own likelihood, which is not calibrated. Use as a ranking aid only.

source: Gruenwald (2004) tutorial, MML and the single-hypothesis problem
finding: MML gives one best hypothesis by an invariant rule. MAP depends on parametrisation and the posterior mean cannot compare model families. Example: phylogenetic trees, where the full posterior is an uninterpretable mixture.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Argument from the Wallace school, reported by an MDL author.
agent_relevance: Supports committing to one explanation by code length when we must act, instead of keeping a blurry mixture.

source: Gruenwald (2004) tutorial, MDL and Bayes
finding: Refined MDL and Bayes factors choose the same model for large enough n in nested cases. MDL is not just a special case of Bayes because it avoids needing a true prior.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Philosophy differs (MML fully Bayesian); practice often similar.
agent_relevance: Links to subfield 05_mdl_and_bayes; nothing new to act on here.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: Large language models plus arithmetic coding are strong general lossless compressors, including on images and audio that are not their training modality.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4 percent and LibriSpeech to 16.4 percent of raw size; PNG gets 58.5 and FLAC 30.3. On enwik9 raw rate: Chinchilla 70B 8.3 percent, Llama 2 7B 8.9, gzip 32.3, LZMA2 23.0.
limits: Raw rate ignores model size. Counted as a two-part code, big models lose. Transformers trained on enwik overfit to text.
agent_relevance: The log-loss of an LLM is a valid code length, so MML-style scoring of text hypotheses is computable with an LLM.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression, two-part versus prequential
finding: The adjusted rate is a two-part code (log-loss plus model size). The paper notes that prequential coding would give better adjusted compression because it charges the training script, not the weights.
numbers: A 38M-parameter transformer on gzip and LZMA2 compressed data reached 92.2 and 89.1 percent (stated in text).
limits: Only the offline setting was computed.
agent_relevance: Charging a whole model as the hypothesis (pure MML two-part view) makes any big model look bad. For an agent, hypothesis cost should be the short written explanation, not the weights.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression, generative use
finding: Any compressor, even gzip, can be run as a conditional generative model, showing prediction and compression are one object.
numbers: Abstract statement; samples shown in paper.
limits: Generations from gzip are poor; it is a demonstration.
agent_relevance: Supports scoring answers by the code length a model assigns, and no more than that.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly
finding: Across public base LLMs, bits per character on fresh domain text predicts average benchmark score almost linearly.
numbers: 31 public LLMs, 12 benchmarks. Pearson about -0.95 in each of three domains (knowledge and commonsense, code, math). Knowledge and commonsense fit: Pearson -0.93, RMSE 3.1 percent.
limits: Base models only; fine-tuned models are not general compressors. Qwen series excluded from the fit: Min-K percent Prob (k=20) suggested contamination on GSM8K and MATH, and they sat above the line.
agent_relevance: Compression is a usable, hard-to-game signal of model quality. It says nothing yet about choosing among answers within one model.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly, corpus size
finding: The compression corpus can be small. Correlation strengthens with size and saturates near 3 million characters (tested 50K to 100M).
numbers: Saturation at about 3M characters; tens of millions are plenty.
limits: Tested on knowledge and commonsense ability only.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-length probe on a few MB of held-out text is enough to compare model variants.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The Description Length of Deep Learning Models
finding: Networks compress their labels well once model cost is counted, but only with prequential (incremental) coding. Variational codes (the Hinton and van Camp lineage, close to MML) give poor bounds. Two-part float32 codes are far worse than uniform.
numbers: MNIST labels: variational 24.1 kbits (ratio 0.12, 95.5 percent test accuracy); prequential 4.10 kbits (ratio 0.021, 99.5 percent), 6 times shorter. CIFAR10: variational 89.0 kbits (ratio 0.54, 61.6 percent); prequential VGGb 45.3 kbits (ratio 0.27, 93 percent), 2 times shorter. 1M parameters at float32 is 32 Mbits, 200 times the uniform code on CIFAR10.
limits: Images, not text. The model with the best variational codelength had low test accuracy, matching the known complaint that Bayesian selection is too conservative compared with cross-validation.
agent_relevance: Strict MML-style hypothesis cost picks too-simple models. Prefer a prequential score (how well earlier evidence predicts later evidence), in line with our held-out rule G3.

source: Voita and Titov (2020) Information-Theoretic Probing with Minimum Description Length
finding: Probe accuracy cannot separate real linguistic structure from memorised control tasks; description length can. Variational (bits-back, MML lineage) and online codes agree.
numbers: ELMo, Penn Treebank part-of-speech. Layer 0: control accuracy 96.3 vs linguistic 93.7, yet control codelength about twice as long. Across 10 probe settings accuracy picked the wrong task in 8, MDL in 0. Control codelengths at least twice the linguistic ones. Pruned probe at layer 1: 664-55-35 units (linguistic) vs 824-272-260 (control).
limits: One task in the main text; ELMo probes, not generation. Their two codes agree, which contradicts Blier and Ollivier's image result; they guess a different variational method.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that effort needed to explain data (code length) catches fits that accuracy on the given data misses. Matches guardrail G3.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Self-Adaptive In-Context Learning: An Information Compression Perspective
finding: Choose and order in-context examples per input by the shortest code length of the model's predicted label distribution (MDL rank). Beats random and entropy-based ranking.
numbers: GPT2-XL (1.5B), 8 datasets. Mean accuracy TopK+MDL 60.16 vs Random 42.78 (+40.4 percent relative), TopK 58.14 (+3.5), TopK+LocalE 51.36 (+17.2), Majority vote 50.43 (+19.3). SST-2 91.51. Lower mean MDL went with higher accuracy.
limits: Small model only. Uses the model's own confidence p(y|c,x) as the code, so confident wrong answers can win.
agent_relevance: A working use of a compression score inside prompting. It ranks by model confidence, which guardrail G5 warns against; use only with an external check.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Self-Adaptive ICL, link to entropy
finding: Their MDL rank equals entropy minimisation when model confidence is the code. This is opposite to the earlier Local Entropy method (Lu et al. 2022), which maximises entropy.
numbers: GlobalE mean 49.75 vs TopK+MDL 60.16.
limits: Confidence-as-code can reward confident wrong answers.
agent_relevance: The same code-length idea ranks prompts in opposite directions depending on how the code is defined. Define the code in program code, not by asking the model.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) LLMZip: Lossless Text Compression using Large Language Models
finding: LLaMA-7B with arithmetic coding compresses English text to about 0.71 bits per character, better than the best classic tools.
numbers: text8 1MB: 0.7101 bpc (batches 0.689 to 0.699); ZPAQ 1.4, paq8h 1.2. Entropy upper bound estimate 0.709 (1MB), 0.85 (100KB). 100KB Gutenberg text: 0.8426 bpc.
limits: Likely optimistic: LLaMA was trained on Wikipedia, from which text8 is derived. Classic baselines were quoted from the literature, not rerun.
agent_relevance: An LLM's log-loss on text is a strong code length, and contamination makes code lengths on known text meaningless.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation
finding: Ask a code model for the shortest program that outputs a data sequence. Flagship models do badly, and the metric is hard to game because the program must run and match exactly.
numbers: Length-128 sequences: Llama-3.1-405B and GPT-4o produce a wrong program on average 78 and 40 percent of the time for natural sequences and 66 and 45 percent for synthetic ones (stated in text). GPT-4o accuracy: audio-16bit 35.6, DNA 24.8, text 6.5. All prompted models have Precision above 1.0, so programs are longer than gzip. Trained SeqCoder-8B reaches compression rate 0.38 on synthetic data, beating gzip.
limits: Gains on synthetic data generalise poorly: trained models score near zero on natural sequences. Chain of thought changed accuracy by -1.3, -5.1 and +2.1 points for 8B, 70B and 405B Llama. Table text was garbled in extraction, so per-cell values are less certain than the prose.
agent_relevance: Direct measure that LLMs are poor at MML-style inference (find the shortest exact explanation). Do not trust a model's claim that its explanation is short; measure it in code.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) Kolmogorov Test, priors and error analysis
finding: The prior over programs matters. A plain uniform prior over a small DSL beat gzip. Inline execution feedback gave only modest gains.
numbers: SeqCoder-1.5B trained on 10K examples: 27.2 percent correct on length-16 audio-MFCC; at length 128 more than 99 percent of its programs err in the first 16 characters. With 100K and 1M training examples, 93.5 and 88.7 percent err early.
limits: One benchmark family. Authors say new methods are needed.
agent_relevance: Confirms the MML point that the code for hypotheses (the prior) decides which explanation wins. Our schema should fix the description language once, in code.

source: Lester et al. (2024) Training LLMs over Neurally Compressed Text
finding: Text compressed by an LLM plus arithmetic coding is not learnable by a second LLM. Equal-Info Windows (blocks that each compress to the same bit count) make it learnable.
numbers: Subword tokenisers give about 4x compression. Equal-Info Windows beat byte-level baselines by a wide margin on bits per byte and improve with scale. EqualInfoAC[b=16, v=65k] is the best compression method.
limits: SentencePiece stays best at equal parameter count; perplexity of compressed-text models is worse.
agent_relevance: Maximal compression destroys learnable structure. A shortest message is a bad working representation for the model; use it as a score only.

source: Heurtel-Depeiges, Ruoss, Veness and Genewein (2025) Compression via Pre-trained Transformers
finding: Small pre-trained transformers (millions of parameters) beat gzip, LZMA2 and domain compressors even when parameter size is counted. Big foundation models cannot.
numbers: Trained on 165GB of bytes (text, image, audio); tested on 1GB out-of-distribution per modality. Best OOD audio ratio 0.49 vs FLAC 0.54. Transfer to unseen modalities is weak.
limits: Not a practical compressor: compute is far above gzip.
agent_relevance: The two-part cost of the model is the binding limit. This is the MML trade-off measured on neural networks.

source: Zheng, Dowe, Peiris and Rosadi (2021) Minimum Message Length in Hybrid ARMA and LSTM Model Forecasting
finding: MML87 selects ARMA orders better than AIC, BIC and HQ, both in plain ARMA and when residuals feed an LSTM. The hybrid MML ARMA-LSTM was best overall.
numbers: Simulation: 10 parameter sets, 100 runs, N = 50 to 500 points, forecast windows T = 3 to 50, RMSE. Real data: 10 Dow Jones stocks, T up to 200. LSTM alone was much worse than ARMA or the hybrid.
limits: Not uniform. ARIMA at T=3: RMSE AIC 2.987, BIC 3.027, HQ 2.914, MML87 3.075 (MML87 worst). Hybrid at T=200: AIC 26.831, BIC 26.424, HQ 26.662, MML87 26.507 (BIC best). Authors say MML wins in most cases only. The authors include the Dowe group that developed MML.
agent_relevance: Honest effect size: MML gains are real in small samples but small and mixed at long horizons. Do not expect a large lift from MML scoring.

source: Fang et al. (2025) Model Selection from Multiple Model Families in Species Distribution Modeling Using MML
finding: MML puts models from different families on one scale and recovers the right feature set more often than AIC, AICc and BIC, and is robust to family misspecification.
numbers: Artificial data: 11 tests; all methods failed one; on the other 10 MML was fully correct while each rival failed on some. Real data: two plant species from Barro Colorado Island; MML chose the simplest model with the best overall prediction.
limits: The paper itself cites a rival study finding model selection gives no significant gain over fitting the most complex model. Few tests; authors from the MML group.
agent_relevance: Evidence that one code length can compare hypotheses of different kinds. Argues for one scoring rule across hypothesis types.

source: Heterogeneous Graphical Granger Causality by Minimum Message Length (2020)
finding: MML in a heterogeneous graphical Granger model fixes overestimation of causal links in short time series. Two algorithms (HMMLGA, exHMML) beat Lingam, HGGM and a statistical Granger framework in synthetic tests.
numbers: Real data: electrohysterogram of Icelandic mothers (pregnancy vs labor, Physionet) and Austrian climate series. The genetic version gave the most realistic results per the authors.
limits: Exact synthetic scores not read this session. Realism judged by the authors.
agent_relevance: MML acts as an anti-overfitting term when evidence is short, which is our situation with few examples.

source: Sharma and King (2026) Compressing Chemistry Reveals Functional Groups
finding: MML-based search for substructures that compress about three million biologically relevant molecules (SMILES) recovers most human-curated functional groups and finds new larger ones.
numbers: 24 bioactivity data sets, 5 repeats of random 75/25 splits, Wilcoxon signed-rank with Benjamini-Hochberg at alpha 0.05. Fingerprints from dataset-specific groups significantly beat MACCS and Morgan with ridge regression. MolFormer-XL embeddings also compared.
limits: Search limited to SMILES substrings, so true substructures are missed. Linear models only. Exact effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: An MML-guided discovery loop works as unsupervised concept finding. The concept list is a reusable data product.

source: Makalic and Schmidt (2026) Information Geometry and Asymptotic Theory for SMML Estimators
finding: Strict MML splits into assertion entropy plus conditional cross-entropy. The best codepoint for each cell is the model distribution that minimises KL from the cell's data distribution.
numbers: Theory paper; no benchmark numbers.
limits: Strict MML is hard to compute; practical MML uses the Wallace-Freeman approximation.
agent_relevance: Theory only; no direct use in an agent.

source: From More Is Different to Algorithmic Emergence (2026)
finding: Proofs that finding a shorter description can take unbounded time and any always-halting search has blind spots. A model can still pay for itself by reuse even if not minimal, when its own cost is counted.
numbers: Three impossibility results and a sufficient certificate in explicit code lengths.
limits: Theory only. Authors say LLM assistants helped draft text and check derivations.
agent_relevance: Supports a budgeted, signal-triggered search for shorter explanations rather than an unbounded one.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: A per-puzzle network trained at test time to minimise a code length (KL of latent plus 10x reconstruction) solves ARC puzzles with no pretraining. Answer chosen by frequency of sampled grids.
numbers: 2000 iterations, about 20 minutes per puzzle on an RTX 4070. Training set pass@2 34.75 (pass@1 30.25, pass@100 48.5); evaluation set pass@2 20 (pass@1 18.5, pass@100 31.25). Total 130 h and 138 h.
limits: Blog, not peer reviewed. No weight regularisation was used. Posterior collapse in some runs gives wrong answers. Fails on counting, rotation, long-range extension. No same-split comparison with LLMs; reasoning models reach 87.5 percent on semi-private at huge compute.
agent_relevance: Closest working MDL-style solver on ARC (see subfields 08 and 09). Compression-driven search is slow but needs no pretraining.

source: Crossref listing of works on 'minimum message length' since 2020 (accessed 2026-11-17)
finding: Recent MML papers are almost all statistics and ML applications: mixture models of rainfall, inflation, mutual funds, Kotz and Dirichlet mixtures, censored exponential, species modelling. I found no paper using MML inside an LLM agent loop.
numbers: 116,189 fuzzy hits; first 20 titles from 2020 to 2025 all non-LLM. Europe PMC open-access hits: 37.
limits: Search tools were limited this session (WebSearch budget used up; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv API returned 429), so coverage is partial and the absence claim is weak.
agent_relevance: Using MML in an LLM agent would be new and untested.

source: Applied MML mixture-model papers 2021-2025 (titles via Crossref)
finding: Typical pattern: MML picks the number of mixture components and avoids overfit, reported by the authors on rainfall, inflation and mutual-fund clustering. Mostly small-conference papers.
numbers: Titles only, no numbers.
limits: Self-reported; no independent replication seen.
agent_relevance: Do not cite these as evidence for LLM use.
